A comprehensive history of Programming Languages & comparison of relative speeds, great read

Interesting read, but I have a few comments on the part about dynamic typing

Compared to static typing, dynamic typing can be more flexible (e.g. by allowing programs to generate types and functionality based on run-time data)

This line is extremely questionable. First it infers that you can do things in dynamically typed languages which aren't feasible or practical in static typing (which is untrue), second it says that programs in dynamic typing generate types which is, as far as I know, never the case (instead they rely on "uni-typing", or groups of types that encompasses a larger set of values by using implicit conversions)

In practice, the testing done to ensure correct program operation can detect a much wider range of errors than static type-checking, but conversely cannot search as comprehensively for the errors that both testing and static type checking are able to detect.

Comparing unit testing to static typing, two completely different things and static typing does not negate the need for unit tests. Unit tests in dynamic typing doesn't remove the benefit of static analysis.

(For the record, I'm an opponent of dynamic typing in general-purpose environments)
